pages.title: Queues - implementation
pages.content:
Let's explain queues with a simple real-world example involving people waiting in line at a bus stop.
- **Introduction to the Queue / The Queue Setup:**\
Queue is a data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle, where the first person (or item) to arrive is the first one to be served or processed - just like in a bus line
- **Enqueuing (Adding to the Queue):**\
People join the queue when they arrive at the bus stop. \
They stand at the end of the line and wait for the bus.
- **Dequeuing (Removing from the Queue):**\
When the bus arrives, the driver opens the door and allows passengers to board in the order they arrived (FIFO).
- **Peeking at the Front Passenger:**\
The driver may want to know who the next passenger is without letting them board yet.
- **Checking If the Queue Is Empty:**\
After the bus departs, the queue may become empty as all passengers have boarded.\
This is useful to determine if more passengers are waiting or if the service (the bus in this case) can close.

### Task

- Given a empty queue, q1.
- Perform the following operation over q1.
- Push(or Enqueue) 5, Push 6, Push 7, Pop (or Dequeue).

**Note left side will be the head of the queue**

pages.title: Step 2 — Build the Mental Model
pages.content:
### Understand before implementing
A stack is LIFO, a queue is FIFO, and a deque supports insertion/removal at both ends.

**Recognition rule**
Match the operation order in the problem to the required access discipline.

**Do not memorize a code template yet.** First identify what state the algorithm must maintain and what information it can safely discard.
pages.teachingGoal: Explain the idea in plain language and identify when it should be considered.

pages.title: Step 3 — Worked Dry Run
pages.content:
### Trace before code
Write the container contents after every push/pop/enqueue/dequeue.

Use a table with four columns:
- **Step / index**
- **Current input/state**
- **Important invariant**
- **Decision / next state**

Then test one boundary case before implementing.
pages.teachingGoal: Trace the state transition without depending on the final code.

pages.title: Step 4 — Guided Build
pages.content:
### Build it in small pieces
Define the empty/full conditions, choose representation, implement operations, then test transitions around empty and single-element states.

**Guided order**
1. Write the inputs and outputs.
2. State the invariant.
3. Write pseudocode.
4. Implement only the first transition.
5. Test on the tiny example.
6. Add the remaining loop/recursion/structure.
7. Test an edge case.
8. State time and space complexity.

**Common trap:** Using the wrong end, incorrect front/rear updates, and empty-container errors.
pages.teachingGoal: Turn the mental model into a correct implementation without jumping straight to a full template.

pages.title: MCQ
pages.content:
What will be the remaining deque after performing the following operations?

Here, we will use 
- push_front(x) - to push x in the front of deque
- push_back(x) -  to push x in the back of deque
- pop_back() - to pop the last element of deque
- pop_front() - to pop the front element of deque


Initially you are given an empty deque.
### Operations
- push_front(5)
- push_back(6)
- push_back(3)
- push_front(5)
- push_front(9)
- pop_back()

***Note the left side will be the front of deque and the right side will be the back of deque***

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in MCQ and choose an implementation that remains correct on edge cases and within the stated complexity.

steps.exitCriteria: I can explain the prerequisite without opening another lesson.

steps.title: Build the mental model
steps.goal: A stack is LIFO, a queue is FIFO, and a deque supports insertion/removal at both ends.
steps.action: Read the concept explanation and identify the input, state, operation, and desired output.
steps.exitCriteria: I can describe what the technique stores/changes and why it exists.

steps.title: Learn when to use it
steps.goal: Match the operation order in the problem to the required access discipline.
steps.action: Classify two short problem statements and name the pattern before looking at solutions.
steps.exitCriteria: I can give at least two signals that this technique applies.

steps.title: Trace a tiny example
steps.goal: Write the container contents after every push/pop/enqueue/dequeue.

steps.exitCriteria: I can predict the final state/output for a small example.

steps.goal: Define the empty/full conditions, choose representation, implement operations, then test transitions around empty and single-element states.

steps.exitCriteria: I can adapt the approach to a changed input or requirement.

steps.goal: Start with the easiest related problem and move toward mixed/harder problems only after explaining the previous solution.

topics.title: Deque & Sliding Window Maximum
topics.description: Maintain candidate maxima so each element enters and leaves once.

pages.title: Prerequisite Check
pages.content:
Before solving Deque & Sliding Window Maximum, confirm the learner can identify the input shape, the operation being requested, and the expected complexity target.

- State the input and output in your own words.
- Identify the simplest correct baseline approach.
- Name the constraint that can make the baseline too slow.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without skipping the required reasoning step.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated visual/state trace for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
Deque & Sliding Window Maximum is easier to master when the rule is reduced to one repeatable mental model. Start with the data state, the operation, and the condition that permits each update.

- Identify the state that must be maintained.
- Write the update rule in one sentence.
- State what must always remain true.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without skipping the required reasoning step.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated visual/state trace for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum.

pages.title: Intuition Before Code
pages.content:
Before implementation, reason about a small example for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum. Ask what information can be reused and what work can safely be skipped.

- What information is repeated?
- What can be maintained incrementally?
- What changes when the input grows by one element?
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without skipping the required reasoning step.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated visual/state trace for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum.

pages.title: Worked Example
pages.content:
Work through a small instance of Deque & Sliding Window Maximum by hand. Do not code yet; write each important state transition.

- Start with the initial state.
- Apply one operation at a time.
- Record the state after every transition.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without skipping the required reasoning step.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated visual/state trace for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
Implement Deque & Sliding Window Maximum in the smallest readable version first. Separate input parsing, algorithm state, and output so debugging is localized.

- Translate the invariant into variables.
- Implement one transition at a time.
- Check the sample immediately after the first implementation.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without skipping the required reasoning step.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated visual/state trace for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum.

pages.title: Independent Practice
pages.content:
Now solve a fresh variation of Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without looking at the reference implementation. Use the same pattern but a different input arrangement or boundary.

- Restate the task.
- Choose the pattern explicitly.
- Predict the output before running.
- Test a minimum, boundary, and adversarial case.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without skipping the required reasoning step.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated visual/state trace for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum.

pages.title: Debugging Lab
pages.content:
Debugging Deque & Sliding Window Maximum should begin with the invariant and boundary conditions, not random edits.

- Check initialization.
- Check loop/condition boundaries.
- Check pointer/state movement.
- Check complexity against constraints.
pages.teachingGoal: By the end of this step, the learner can progress through Deque & Sliding Window Maximum without skipping the required reasoning step.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated visual/state trace for Deque & Sliding Window Maximum.

pages.title: Mastery Gate
pages.content:
You have mastered Deque & Sliding Window Maximum when you can explain the pattern, implement it from scratch, and transfer it to a new problem with the same underlying idea.

- Explain the invariant without code.
- Implement from a blank editor.
- Give time and space complexity.
- Name one common failure mode.
